title: Magandiya (Sn 4.9)
hookLine: read it: the Buddha refuses a marriage offer and speaks of inner peace
tomorrow: what does a person at peace look like, right before the end?

lines: AN AUNT WITH A PHONE FULL OF PHOTOS.
SO WHAT DO YOU HOLD TO?
cards: Some families hire a matchmaker. Some just have an aunt with a phone full of photos and a very good feeling about somebody's nephew. The ninth poem in the chapter of eights opens with a match.
A brahmin named Magandiya brings his daughter, beautiful and sought after, and offers her to the Buddha as a wife. The Buddha says no, bluntly, in words some readers find harsh.
Then Magandiya asks the question the rest of the poem answers: so what do you hold to?

teach.h: 'I DECLARE THIS' DOESN'T COME TO ME.
teach.b: In paraphrase from the Sutta Nipata. Magandiya wants a position: what view, what practice, what kind of life do you teach? The Buddha's reply is strange.
The thought I declare this doesn't come to me, he says.

teach.h: NOT BY VIEWS. NOT WITHOUT THEM.
teach.b: Looking into views without grasping them, I saw inner peace. Magandiya presses: how do the wise describe this inner peace? Not by view, learning, knowledge, or rules and vows, the Buddha says.
And not without them, either. Let them go without clinging, and be at peace. Magandiya calls that confused, even foolish.
The Buddha answers gently that he's asking from inside his own views and getting tangled in them. Then the picture.

A lotus grows in water, its stem rough, and the water and mud don't stain it. So the sage, who speaks of peace, isn't stained by wanting or by the world. Here's what makes this poem useful on a hard week.

teach.h: NOT AN ANSWER: A WAY OF HOLDING.
teach.b: Inner peace isn't an answer you finally get.
It isn't the right opinion, or the good news. It's a way of holding, in the middle of the mud, while the answer hasn't come.

how: Buddhist teachers use the lotus, rooted in mud and unstained by it, as a picture of living at peace in the middle of ordinary life; the lotus appears in Buddhist art across many countries.

o: a brahmin who asks what the Buddha holds to
a monk well-known for perfect meditation
a queen who gave the Buddha a lotus garden

games.q: inside the poem — tap the pairs.
p: offers his daughter as a wife
a thought that doesn't come to him
not by views, nor without them

s: the Buddha says inner peace comes from holding the right view
not by view, learning or rules, he says, and not without them: by letting go of clinging.
Magandiya calls the Buddha's answer foolish
and the Buddha says he's tangled in his own views as he asks.
the poem pictures the sage as a lotus unstained by mud
born in water, rough-stemmed, and not soiled by the water or the mud.

games.q: a friend says she'll finally be calm once she figures out the right thing to believe about everything. by the poem, what's missing?
o: peace isn't won by a view; it's in not clinging, even to views.
nothing; once her views are all correct, the peace will follow.
she should drop every belief; having no views is the peace.
games.why: the poem rules out both: not by views, and not without them. the third option is the skimmer's trap. peace is in the not-clinging.

practice: Pick one sound in the room, the hum of a fridge, traffic, a bird, your own breath, and rest your attention on it. Each time the mind runs ahead to an answer you're waiting for, notice it, and come back to the sound.
Let the waiting happen in the mud while you stay with the sound.

wordCard.voice: Magandiya: the brahmin who offers his daughter, then asks what the Buddha holds to, and hears about an inner peace that isn't one more view.

orig.note: Pali: the name of the brahmin in this poem, the Māgandiya Sutta.

carryVoice: Here's the line: inner peace, which doesn't wait for the answer to arrive. That's poem nine.
